DATA 308: Homework 3

Simple linear regression

Author

Dylan Wikel

Please change the author name to your own. Answer in complete sentences.

Bike share data

We have data on bike ridership among registered members of the Capital Bikeshare service in Washington, D.C. rentals by weather.

Question 0

Begin by running the code chunk below to load the tidyverse package and the bikes data from the bayesrules package. You may need to first install the packages using install.packages(c("tidyverse", "bayesrules")) in the Console.

library(tidyverse)
library(bayesrules)

data("bikes")

Question 1

Type ?bikes into the Console to view the data documentation. What is the description of the variables called rides and temp_actual?

Response

rides refers to the number of bikeshare rides and temp_actual refers to raw temperature measured in degrees Fahrenheit.

Question 2

We want to explore if we can use the temperature to predict the number of daily bikeshare rides we will get. Produce a plot to visualize the relationship between rides and temp_actual. Make sure to provide axes labels instead of just using the default labels. (Hint: Look at slide 10 of lecture 4a.)

Response

ggplot(bikes, 
       aes(x = rides,
           y = temp_actual)
       ) + 
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of Bikeshare Rides",
    y = "Temperature in Degrees Fahrenheit",
    title = "The Relationship Between Number of Bikeshare Rides and Temperature"
  )

Question 3

Reproduce your plot from question 2, but now add a linear regression line to the plot. Does it appear to model your data well?

Response

ggplot(bikes, 
       aes(x = rides,
           y = temp_actual)
       ) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              color = "purple"
              ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of Bikeshare Rides",
    y = "Temperature in Degrees Fahrenheit",
    title = "The Relationship Between Number of Bikeshare Rides and Temperature"
  )

The regression line models the data fairly well. I can see that there is a positive relationship between temp_actual and rides such that as temp_actual increases, rides also increases.

Question 4

Fit a linear model to regress rides on temp_actual, saving your model as bike_model. Note, I did not provide a code chunk for you to use for this question. You will have to click the “+C” button at the top of this document to add an R code chunk.

Response

bike_model <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual, data = bikes)

summary(bike_model)

Call:
lm(formula = rides ~ temp_actual, data = bikes)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3564.3 -1009.3  -116.4   959.1  3184.6

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)

temp_actual    89.23       5.67  15.739  < 2e-16 ***
---

Multiple R-squared:  0.3322,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3308 
F-statistic: 247.7 on 1 and 498 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

Question 5

Specify the fitted model in context.

Response

\[\hat Y{Rides_i} = -2168.77 + 89.23(Temperature_i)\]

Question 6

Interpret the estimate for the y-intercept in context. Does it have a meaningful interpretation in this context?

Response

The expected number of ride when temp_actual is equal to 0 is -2168.77 rides. This does not have meaningful interpretation in context as there are no recorded values in temp_actual equal to 0 and we would not expect a negative number of rides as it is impossible.

Question 7

Interpret the estimate for the slope in context.

Response

The slope in this context is 89.23. For each unit increase in temp_actual, we expect an increase in ride by 89.23.

Question 8

Identify the 95% confidence interval for the slope and its corresponding margin of error.

Response

ci_bike <- confint(bike_model)["temp_actual", ]

# margin of error
bike_me <- (ci_bike[2] - ci_bike[1]) / 2 

ci_bike
   2.5 %   97.5 % 
 78.0944 100.3734 
bike_me
  97.5 % 
11.13949

Question 9

Improve your interpretation from question 7 here by adding the margin of error and confidence level into your interpretation.

Response

A 1 degree increase in temp_actual is associated with an increase in bikeshare rides of 89.23 plus or minus 11.13949 rides with 95% confidence.

Question 10

What daily number of rides would our model predict for a day where the temperature is 70 degrees Fahrenheit?

Response

temp_data <- data.frame(temp_actual = 70)

predict(bike_model, newdata = temp_data, interval = "confidence")
       fit      lwr      upr
1 4077.598 3942.193 4213.004
predict(bike_model, newdata = temp_data, interval = "prediction")
       fit      lwr      upr
1 4077.598 1543.132 6612.065

Question 11

Identify the 95% interval for your prediction in question 10 and its corresponding margin of error.

Response

For a 70 degree day, we expect 4077.598 bikeshare rides, between 3942.193 and 4213.004 rides, with 95% confidence.

Question 12

Provide an interpretation of your prediction and interval from questions 10 and 11 in context, including your margin of error and confidence level into your interpretation.

Response

For a 70 degree day, we predict 4077.598 bikeshare rides, between 1543.132 and 6612.065 rides, with 95% confidence.
